g.passage: Cape Town had turned cold for the funeral, and in their grandmother's yard the hives sat under sheets like furniture in a closed house. Harriet pressed a parcel into Rangi's hands before the mourners had finished their tea. Inside was a jar of honey with a hand-lettered label: Orange Blossom, Gran's last harvest. Rangi knew at once that it was not; the hives had been empty since winter, and the lid came from the supermarket. He held the jar to the window anyway and said the color was exactly right. Harriet smiled too widely and agreed. Later, when an aunt asked to taste it, Rangi said he was saving it, and Harriet looked at him with something close to gratitude. Along the fence, a row of agapanthus nodded blue heads against the wet brick.

Two cousins quietly sustain a well-meant pretense for each other's sake.

g.passage: Steam and the smell of frying garlic filled the galley where I mended the crew's uniforms while our ship sat in Shanghai for repairs. Meilin, my only apprentice, worked across the table on a torn cuff. That morning the cook, Burak, had burned his hand, and we had both seen it happen. By noon the captain wanted statements. Meilin said the pan had slipped; I had seen Burak reach for it without a cloth. We argued quietly, needles moving. I assumed she was protecting him. Then she described the angle of the handle and the jolt of the hull against the pier, details I had missed because I had been watching his face. We wrote two accounts and signed both. Outside the porthole, gulls fought over a crust on the black water.

options: To recount how a ship's cook burned his hand while the vessel was docked
To describe the daily routine of mending uniforms in a crowded ship's galley
To show the narrator realizing that a conflicting account reflected another view
To argue that witnesses should always trust their own eyes over others' words

g.passage: Lucius found his son already in the backyard vineyard the morning after the storm, kneeling where the wind had torn out the oldest vine behind their South Side two-flat. Its roots had pulled up a rusted lunchbox. "Leave it," Lucius said, but the boy had already pried it open. Inside lay a photograph of Lucius at nineteen, grinning on a club stage with a trumpet, and a ticket stub from Forty-Seventh Street. For years Lucius had told his son, who practiced guitar behind a closed door, that music was no way to feed a family. The boy looked at the photograph a long time, then set it on the fence post and began pressing soil back around the roots. Next door, Beulah called over to ask whether the grapes had survived, and Lucius said most of them had.

He suspects the rusted lunchbox belonged to an earlier owner of the two-flat.

g.passage: Nobody had expected Kenji to come. The fishing season had been the worst in twenty years, and in October he had told Sakura he would leave her boat for a factory job in Sapporo. Yet here he stood at the back of the crowded wedding hall in a borrowed suit, holding a gift wrapped in newspaper. Sakura, who had taught him to mend nets since he was fifteen, watched him search the crowd until he found her nephew, the groom. Kenji had once told her that the boy was the only one in the harbor who never laughed at his clumsy knots. He handed over the parcel, bowed deeply, and slipped out before the speeches. Snow had begun falling on the parking lot, softening the outlines of the delivery vans.

He needs to deliver a gift on behalf of his new factory in Sapporo.
He wishes to apologize to the harbor for the season's poor catch.

g.passage: Kerala's monsoon was drumming on the tin roof of the school music room when Arjun found me there, tuning the harmonium I had sold him a year before. I run the instrument shop by the bus stand, and the school calls me for repairs. All that spring Arjun had come into my shop each week, insisting that the harmonium's flat reed had cost his daughter her place in the state competition. Every time, I had refused to admit fault. That afternoon he did not mention the competition. Instead he pointed to Theo, a boy who would compete next month on an instrument no better than his daughter's, and asked whether I could teach him to hear a reed going flat before a judge did. I said yes before I had decided to. Rain kept pooling under the door, and the caretaker laid sacks across the threshold.

He hopes to earn a refund for his daughter by bringing the shop a new customer.
He wants to keep another young player from losing to a flaw no one noticed.
He has been asked by the school to find a qualified music teacher for Theo.

g.passage: By six the bus to the hills was already late, and Dolores stood under the shelter with a cement-gray handprint still on her shirt. That morning, in front of the whole crew, she had backed the mixer into the site office and knocked the foreman's lunch off the windowsill. Armand had stared at the spilled rice for a long moment. Now he arrived at the stop, set down his bag, and offered her half of a roti he had bought to replace it. "Office needed a new door anyway," he said. She laughed, then covered her mouth, still half ashamed, and he laughed louder so that she would not have to stop. Below them the lights of Port of Spain came on in loose strings, and a dog trotted past with great purpose.

g.passage: Mumbai was still gray when Tara let herself into her uncle's bakery through the back door, the ovens ticking as they warmed. Coach Riccardo was already there, as he was every Saturday, buying pav for the team. He did not look up from the trays. So the rumor had reached him: that she had called his lineup a joke in front of the selectors. She had said the words, though not about him. Tara tied on an apron and began dusting loaves, flour rising in small clouds, and the silence stretched until her hands ached from working. At last Riccardo asked whether the cardamom buns were fresh. She said they would be in ten minutes. He said he would wait. Outside, a delivery boy leaned his bicycle against the shutter and counted coins into his palm.

Mostly at ease, though briefly interrupted by a flicker of strain

g.passage: Because a flooded road was holding up the buses, Niamh and Rory were the only two left in the camp dining hall in Galway, each at the far end of a long table. They had not spoken all week. g.passage: Folasade read the last of their mother's letters aloud while Obinna sat by the guesthouse window, where the monks' bell rope hung motionless in the noon heat of Dakar. The plan had succeeded: the house in Lagos was sold, the debts were paid, and their mother would join them before the rains. Every letter said she was grateful. Not one said she was glad. Between the final pages Folasade found a pressed hibiscus, faded to the color of weak tea, which their mother had always picked from the vine beside the old front door. Obinna turned it over in his palm and remarked that the new house had no such vine. "We can plant one," Folasade said. He laid the flower on the windowsill, and neither of them moved to return it to the envelope, though the breeze kept nudging it toward the edge.

options: the debts that the sale of the house in Lagos has finally settled.
the quiet routine of the monks that the siblings hope to imitate.
the new house that the mother will soon share with her children.
the attachment to home that the mother gave up for the siblings' plan.
g.explanation: 히비스커스는 어머니가 옛집 현관 옆 덩굴에서 늘 따던 꽃이고, 편지에는 고맙다는 말만 있을 뿐 기쁘다는 말은 없다. Obinna가 새집에는 그런 덩굴이 없다고 말하는 대목까지 이어 보면, 이 꽃은 계획을 위해 어머니가 포기한 집에 대한 애착을 나타내므로 D가 정답이다. A는 매각의 결과, B는 배경 소재, C는 꽃과 반대되는 새집을 가리켜 맞지 않는다.

seed.conflict: over how to mark an anniversary
seed.topicSeed: a cemetery gate in Bergen; a young apprentice and a master carpenter over how to mark an anniversary

g.passage: Astrid did not believe in new gates. For forty years she had repaired the oak gate of the cemetery in Bergen, replacing one rotten slat at a time, so that by now hardly a board of the original remained. Her apprentice, Anahera, wanted to mark the gate's hundredth year with something grand: a carved arch, the town's name in gold leaf. Astrid only handed her a plane and a single slat cut from the same stand of oak. "One board," she said. "Each year, one board." Anahera fitted it beside a slat that Astrid's own teacher had set, and the grain of the two ran nearly together. That evening the gate swung shut behind the last mourners, and the hinges, oiled that morning, made no sound at all.
g.question: In the text, the cemetery gate most likely symbolizes
options: a tradition kept alive through small renewals passed between generations.
the private grief of the mourners who visit the cemetery every evening.
Anahera's desire to bring bold and visible changes to the old town.
the gradual decline of careful craftsmanship in a modernizing city.
g.explanation: 문은 한 번에 한 장씩 판자를 갈아 원래 판자가 거의 남지 않았지만 여전히 같은 문으로 서 있다. Astrid는 화려한 기념물 대신 해마다 한 장씩이라는 방식을 전하고, Anahera의 판자가 Astrid의 스승이 끼운 판자 옆에 결이 이어지듯 놓이므로 문은 세대를 거쳐 조금씩 새로워지며 이어지는 전통을 상징한다. 따라서 A가 정답이다. B와 D는 지문에 근거가 약하고, C는 Astrid가 받아들이지 않은 Anahera의 처음 계획일 뿐이다.
